title: The last resort
hookLine: if nothing else works, clench the teeth, tongue to palate, and hold the mind down (MN 20)

cards: Every good toolbox has a crowbar at the bottom. You don't start with it. You try the screwdriver, the wrench, the gentle tap of a hammer, a little oil on the hinge.
But some days, something is really stuck, and you're glad the crowbar is there. MN 20 has one too. It's the fifth of five ways with an unwanted thought, and the Buddha puts it last on purpose.

teach.b: Day three hundred eighty-five walked through all five; here they are again, quickly, to show where the fifth sits. First, the finer peg: another theme, connected with the wholesome.
If that fails, look at the danger in the thought, the way a young person who loves fine clothes would recoil if someone hung the carcass of a snake around their neck.
Third, stop giving the thought attention, the way you'd shut your eyes or look away.
Fourth, calm it step by step, like someone walking fast who asks, why am I hurrying? and slows down, then stands, then sits, then lies down.

And only if all four fail, the fifth: with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, beat down, constrain and crush mind with mind, the way a strong man might hold down a weaker one by the head or shoulders.
It's startling language, and the text doesn't soften it: some days nothing gentle works.

teach.h: MASTER OF THE COURSES OF THOUGHT.
teach.b: But it sits last. And in MN 36, describing his years of harsh practice before his awakening, the Buddha says he tried exactly this, teeth clenched, mind crushing mind, until sweat poured from his armpits.
So force has a place on the path, but a small one, at the bottom of the box.
The discourse ends with a promise: someone who has these five is a master of the courses of thought, thinking what they wish to think, and not what they don't.

how: Teachers who use MN 20 present its five methods in the sutta's order, from the gentlest to the most forceful, keeping the last for when the others have failed.

o: the fifth tool in MN 20: force, kept for last
the first tool to reach for with any thought
a tool for prying open a locked mind

games.q: match each way to its picture in MN 20.
p: a snake's carcass around the neck
walk slower, stand, sit, lie down

s: MN 20 puts the forceful method first
it's fifth, after four gentler ways.
the fourth way slows a thought the way a hurrying walker slows to a stop
walk slowly, stand, sit, lie down.
in MN 36, clenching and crushing the mind brought the Buddha awakening
he says it brought sweat and pain, not awakening.

games.q: you've tried the finer peg, seeing the danger, looking away and slowing down. the thought still won't let go. what does MN 20 say?
o: teeth clenched, tongue to palate, hold the mind down
follow the thought wherever it goes
games.why: only then, the last resort: hold the mind down with the mind. it's there for when nothing else works.

practice: No clenching today, just the spirit of the fifth tool: staying. Bring to mind one small hard moment and, if the body tightens, breathe through it: in, and a long, slow out.
Don't fix it, don't argue with it, don't run; hold steady, breath after breath, until it eases even a little.

wordCard.voice: Crowbar. When gentler ways fail, hold steady and hold the mind down: the fifth tool, kept for last.

orig.note: Pali dantehi dantam ādhāya: with teeth set on teeth; the opening of the last resort in MN 20.

carryVoice: Your line: a tool kept for last. The gentle ways come first, every time. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 20, Vitakkasanthana Sutta (the five methods)
Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the ascetic struggle)
